960.title: Tagore's Gitanjali (public domain, 1912)
960.hook: a small reed flute, carried over hills, played by someone else's breath
960.howItsDone: Tagore wrote the Gitanjali songs in Bengali, and in Bengal his songs are still sung at home, in schools and at gatherings; readers elsewhere often know the poems through his own English prose versions.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Gandhi's Gita with the person of steady wisdom: the tortoise drawing in, the sea staying level while the rivers pour in. Did you draw in like the tortoise? Today, a poet. Day nine hundred sixty.

A reed flute is a plain thing. A hollow stalk, a few holes, nothing inside. It makes no sound on its own. Somebody has to pick it up, carry it, and breathe through it, and then a song comes out that the reed could never have made by itself. Hold that picture, because a poet opened a book with it. The English edition of his songs carries a short subtitle, Song Offerings, and says it was translated by the author from the original Bengali. The poet is Rabindranath Tagore. The book is Gitanjali. And its very first poem turns on an empty vessel and a little flute.
screen: `A REED FLUTE MAKES NO SOUND ALONE.` → `SONG OFFERINGS.` → `TAGORE'S GITANJALI.`

segments.voice: Here is how the first poem opens, in Tagore's own English: "Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life." Notice who is doing the work. The speaker doesn't fill himself. He is emptied, and filled, by someone he addresses only as thou. Then the flute arrives. The poem says this little reed has been carried over hills and dales, and that thou has breathed through it melodies always new. So the singer of these songs is, in his own picture, the instrument and not the musician. That turns the title around. A song offering sounds like something a person makes and hands up to God. But in the first poem, the songs were breathed in from the other side first. What gets offered back is what was given. The poem ends on hands. It says the infinite gifts come only on these very small hands, and that ages pass, and still thou pourest, and still there is room to fill. Small hands, an endless pouring, and room left over. Why does this belong in a Hindu path, among the modern teachers? Because it keeps company with old things. A singer who pours out songs to a divine thou is close to the bhakti poets, who sang to God as a lover or a friend. And the vessel emptied and refilled sits near the Gita's teaching we just spent days on: the work is done, the fruit is let go, and something keeps flowing through. Tagore doesn't name a god in this poem, and doesn't argue. He just says thou, and keeps listening. Some readers hear Krishna in it, some hear the one Self of the Upanishads, some simply hear a person grateful to be alive.
screen: `EMPTIED AND FILLED AGAIN.` · `THE SINGER IS THE FLUTE, NOT THE PLAYER.` · `WHAT IS OFFERED WAS GIVEN FIRST.` · `SMALL HANDS, ENDLESS POURING.` · then, large: `STILL THERE IS ROOM TO FILL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up. Small hands. Breathe out fully, as if the vessel is being emptied. Then let the next breath come in on its own, without pulling it. Notice that you didn't make it. It arrived. Stay with that for a while: out, emptied; in, filled again. If you pray, you can hold the breath that comes in as the gift the poem talks about. If not, just notice that there is still room for one more. The bell holds the time.
Tagore's Gitanjali. Song offerings, from a poet who pictures himself as a reed flute, emptied and filled again by the one he calls thou.
Your line: still room to fill. Today, when something good comes to you, a meal, a kind word, a quiet minute, notice it came in on small hands. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: Tagore's Gitanjali (public domain, 1912)
961.hook: a poet tells a worshiper to open the temple doors and look outside
961.howItsDone: Hindus pray in many ways, with beads and chanting in a temple corner as well as through daily work, and Tagore's poem is one poet's voice within the tradition, often read as a call to find God among working people.

segments.voice: Yesterday we opened Tagore's Gitanjali at its first poem: the frail vessel emptied and filled, the little reed flute, and still room to fill. What came to you on small hands? Day nine hundred sixty-one.

A dark corner of a temple. The doors are shut. Someone sits there with a string of beads, chanting, eyes closed. It's a real and honored form of devotion. And in one of the Gitanjali poems, the poet walks up to that person and says, in effect: stop for a moment. Open your eyes. Your God isn't before you. It's a startling thing for a devotional poet to say. Today, poem eleven, and where Tagore says to look instead.
screen: `A DARK CORNER, DOORS SHUT.` → `OPEN YOUR EYES.` → `WHERE TO LOOK INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Here are the poem's opening lines, in Tagore's own English: "Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!" Then he says where God is: "He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones." A farmer in a field. A laborer on a road. The poem goes on to say that God is with them in sun and in shower, with his garment covered in dust. And it tells the worshiper to put off the holy mantle and come down onto the dusty soil too. It's worth being careful about what this poem is doing. It doesn't sneer at the worshiper. But it does say plainly: leave the beads, and later, leave the flowers and incense too. Its sharpest picture is the shut doors. A devotion that walls itself off from the people working in the sun has, in this poem, missed where God already is. Tagore's family belonged to the Brahmo Samaj, a reform movement wary of image worship, and the poem carries that voice. Hindus who pray with beads and flowers may answer that their worship is where they learn to see God in the field. And then comes a surprising line. The worshiper hopes for deliverance, for freedom from all this. The poem asks where such deliverance is to be found, since the master himself has joyfully taken on the bonds of creation. God isn't escaping the world. God is bound up in it, on purpose, gladly. The poem closes by telling the worshiper to meet him and stand by him in toil and in the sweat of the brow. In Tagore's poem the place of worship and the place of work turn out to be the same place.
screen: `LEAVE THE CHANTING, OPEN YOUR EYES.` · `GOD IS WITH THE TILLER AND THE PATHMAKER.` · `THE COMPLAINT IS THE SHUT DOOR.` · `GOD HAS TAKEN ON THE BONDS OF CREATION.` · then, large: `MEET HIM IN TOIL.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and if your eyes are closed, open them. Let your gaze rest on whatever is in front of you. Then bring to mind someone whose work you depend on and rarely see: whoever grew the food you ate today, whoever laid the road outside, whoever cleans the building. Picture them at it, in sun or in rain. Stay with one of them. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, right where they are working. If not, simply keep them in view, with some gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Tagore's Gitanjali. In poem eleven, the doors come open, and God is found where the tiller tills and the pathmaker breaks stones.
Your line: God with the tiller. Today, look up once at someone working, a driver, a cook, a cashier, and let them be the place the poem points to. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

962.title: Tagore's Gitanjali (public domain, 1912)
962.hook: a prayer that is one long sentence, made of the word where
962.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
962.howItsDone: Poem 35 of Gitanjali, 'Where the mind is without fear', is one of the poems some readers learn by heart and recite, at school or at gatherings about freedom and education.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Tagore's Gitanjali, the temple doors came open: God with the tiller and the pathmaker, garment covered in dust. Whose work did you look up and see? Day nine hundred sixty-two.

Where. It's a small word, usually a question. Where are my keys. Where did the afternoon go. In one Gitanjali poem, Tagore takes that word and stacks it, line on line, where, where, where, like someone describing a place they long to live in. Only at the very end does the sentence land, and it turns out the whole thing was a prayer. Today, poem thirty-five, our last day with Tagore, and the place he asks to wake up in.
screen: `WHERE. A SMALL WORD.` → `LINE ON LINE: WHERE, WHERE, WHERE.` → `THE SENTENCE LANDS AS A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's how it begins, in Tagore's own English: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls." It goes on like that. A place where words come from the depth of truth. Where tireless striving reaches toward perfection. Where the clear stream of reason hasn't lost its way in the dry desert sand of dead habit. Notice that the lines describe conditions of mind and spirit, not buildings or borders. Fear, a head held up or bowed down, walls that split people into fragments, habit that dries reason out. And then the last line turns the whole sentence toward someone: "Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake." My Father. So the poem was addressed all along, just like the first poem with its thou. It isn't a speech about a nation. It's a request, made to God, that a people wake up into a certain kind of freedom. Readers have heard this poem in more than one way. Some hear it about a country and its future. Some hear it about any single person, waking from fear and habit. The poem lets both stand. One more line deserves a slow look, because it points at where this path goes next. Just before the end, the poem asks for a place where the mind is led forward by thee into ever-widening thought and action. Thought and action, led forward by God. Over three days, Tagore has given us a flute breathed through, a God found in the dust of work, and a mind that wakes into freedom. Tomorrow we go back to the Gita, slowly, to the chapters about action itself.
screen: `WHERE THE MIND IS WITHOUT FEAR.` · `STATES OF MIND, NOT BORDERS.` · `MY FATHER, LET MY COUNTRY AWAKE.` · `LED FORWARD INTO THOUGHT AND ACTION.` · then, large: `INTO THAT HEAVEN OF FREEDOM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and lift the head a little, so the chin is level and the neck is long. The head held high, without strain. Breathe. Then go through the poem's wheres, one at a time, and ask each one gently of yourself. Where is there fear in me right now? Where is a narrow wall? Where has a habit gone dry? Don't fix anything. Just notice, and let the breath keep moving. If you pray, you can end with the poem's own last line: into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake. The bell holds the time.
Tagore's Gitanjali. A flute breathed through, God in the dust of work, and a mind waking into freedom, all of it offered back as song.
Your line: into thought and action. Today, catch one moment where fear or plain habit is making the choice, and let the head come up before you act. Day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
963.hook: Arjuna catches his teacher in what looks like a contradiction
963.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
963.howItsDone: Some Hindus begin a day's work, or a meal, by mentally offering it to God, and some Gita study groups read chapter three alongside a classical commentary such as Shankara's.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Tagore's Gitanjali with a prayer made of wheres, and a mind led forward into thought and action. Where did your head come up? Today, a new part of the path. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

If understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible deed? That, in paraphrase, is how chapter three of the Gita begins. Arjuna has been listening closely. In chapter two, Krishna praised a steady understanding and said plain action falls far below it. And all along, he had been telling Arjuna to stand up and fight. Arjuna is confused, and a little irritated. Your words seem mixed, he says. Tell me the one thing that's good for me. We've read these chapters before. Now we read them again, slowly, with the old commentators at our elbow, starting with that complaint.
screen: `WHY PUSH ME INTO THIS DEED?` → `YOUR WORDS SEEM MIXED.` → `READ AGAIN, WITH COMMENTARY.`

segments.voice: Krishna's first answer is almost blunt. Nobody, he says, can stay even for a moment without acting. Every being is made to act by the forces of its own nature. Sitting still is an act. Breathing is an act. Even keeping the body alive, he says a few verses later, couldn't happen without action. So the choice in front of Arjuna was never action or no action. That door doesn't exist. The real question is what kind of action. And here Krishna brings in an old word: yajna, sacrifice, offering. The world, he says, is bound by action, except action done as offering. Do your work in that spirit, free of clinging. Then he tells a short creation story. In the beginning, the Creator brought forth beings together with sacrifice and said: by this you will flourish. You nourish the gods, and the gods will nourish you. Rain, food, work, offering, rain again. Krishna calls it a wheel, set turning, and he says that a person who takes from it and doesn't help turn it lives in vain. So karma, in chapter three, is first of all the plain word for action, and only then the web of consequences it sets going. Action you can't avoid, done as an offering, keeps the wheel turning instead of binding you to it. The commentators lean in at different places. Shankara, glossing the word sacrifice in this verse, says it means the Lord himself, and quotes an older Vedic line that says sacrifice is Vishnu. So for him, action done as offering means action done for God. Other readers keep the word closer to the ritual fire and the shared work of a household. Either way, the verse says the same thing about the doer: act, and let go of the grip.
screen: `NOBODY STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.` · `THE QUESTION IS WHAT KIND OF ACTION.` · `ACTION DONE AS OFFERING DOESN'T BIND.` · `THE WHEEL: NOURISH AND BE NOURISHED.` · then, large: `HELP THE WHEEL TURN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. For the first few breaths, try to do nothing at all. Notice that you can't. The breath goes on, the heart goes on, the body keeps its balance. Action is already happening. Then turn to the wheel. Ask where, in an ordinary day, you mostly take from it and give little back. Don't judge it. Just find one place, and one small way to put something back: refill what you emptied, return what you borrowed, feed what feeds you. If you pray, you can hold that small return before Krishna, or the one you pray to. The bell holds the time.
Karma. In chapter three, first the plain word for action, which nobody escapes, and action done as offering, which keeps the wheel turning.
Your line: keeps the wheel turning. Today, put one thing back into the wheel: refill what you emptied, or return what you borrowed. Day nine hundred sixty-three.

964.title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
964.hook: a king who reached the highest goal without leaving the palace
964.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
964.howItsDone: Some Hindus who study the Gita point to King Janaka as the model of a person who lives in the world and knows the Self, and some study circles dwell on the verse on one's own dharma (3.35).

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma in chapter three: nobody stays a moment without acting, and action done as offering keeps the wheel turning. Which task did you offer? Day nine hundred sixty-four.

Janaka was a king. He had a palace, a court, a kingdom to run, taxes and quarrels and harvests. And in the Hindu tradition he is remembered as a sage, someone who knew the Self while sitting on a throne. Halfway through chapter three, Krishna reaches for his name. Janaka and others like him, Krishna says, reached perfection through action itself. Not by walking away. By doing the work. It's a quiet line, but it opens the second half of the chapter, and a word that holds the whole world together.
screen: `JANAKA: A KING AND A SAGE.` → `PERFECTION THROUGH ACTION.` → `A WORD THAT HOLDS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: The word is lokasangraha. Loka is the world, the people in it. Sangraha is a holding together, a gathering. Krishna tells Arjuna to act with that in view: the holding together of the world. Then he gives the reason, and it's a very human one. Whatever a leading person does, others do too. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. So the way you work isn't private. Somebody is watching it and copying it. Then Krishna points at himself. There is nothing in the three worlds, he says, that I have to do, nothing I lack, nothing I need to gain. And yet I keep acting. If I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart. So, he says, the wise should act without attachment, just as the unwise act with it, for the sake of holding the world together. And the wise shouldn't unsettle the minds of people who are attached to their work. Let them keep working, and show them how by example. A few verses later comes this line: better one's own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's dharma done well. Your own work, your own place in the holding-together, even if it's clumsy. Commentators have weighed this differently. Shankara, who holds that liberation finally comes through knowledge, reads the call to act here as fitting for those still on the way, and as an example for others. Some modern readers took lokasangraha as close to the heart of the whole Gita. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his long commentary called the Gita Rahasya, read it that way, as a charge to keep working for the world's welfare. The verses can carry both. And either way, karma here isn't only my action. It's my action as one thread in a cloth that a lot of other people are wearing.
screen: `LOKASANGRAHA: HOLDING THE WORLD TOGETHER.` · `WHAT A LEADER DOES, OTHERS FOLLOW.` · `KRISHNA NEEDS NOTHING, AND STILL ACTS.` · `BETTER YOUR OWN DHARMA, IMPERFECT.` · then, large: `ONE THREAD IN THE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind the people who see how you work: a child, a coworker, a younger sibling, a neighbor, a friend. You don't need to picture them watching closely. Just notice that they're there. Then think of one thing you do every day, the dishes, a meeting, a commute, and ask what it teaches without a word. Don't judge it. Just see it as one thread in the cloth. If you pray, you can offer that one thread. The bell holds the time.
Karma. Action done for lokasangraha, the holding together of the world, the way King Janaka did it, and the way Krishna says he does.
Your line: hold the world together. Today, do one ordinary piece of your own work carefully, as if someone younger were learning it from you. Day nine hundred sixty-four.

965.title: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
965.hook: the sun, a king, his son, and a teaching handed down until it was lost
965.carry: a teaching lost and told again
965.tomorrow: karma: the Gita ch. 3, 4, 5 re-read with commentary
965.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching lineages, a teaching is received from a teacher in an unbroken parampara, and Gita 4.7–8, 'whenever dharma declines', is a verse some Hindus learn by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma as lokasangraha: King Janaka working his way to perfection, and action done to hold the world together. Who might have learned something from how you worked? Day nine hundred sixty-five.

The sun. Manu. Ikshvaku. Three names, at the start of chapter four, and they're a chain. Krishna says he taught this yoga, the yoga of action he's been explaining, to Vivasvan, the sun. Vivasvan told it to Manu. Manu told it to his son Ikshvaku. And so it was handed on, from one royal sage to the next. Then, Krishna says, over a long stretch of time, it was lost. That's why he's telling it again, now, to Arjuna, on a battlefield. Today, a teaching with a family tree.
screen: `THE SUN, MANU, IKSHVAKU.` → `HANDED ON, KING TO KING.` → `LOST, AND TOLD AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The Gita has a word for this handing on: parampara, one after another, teacher to student. It's how the yoga of action is said to have reached Arjuna. And Krishna tells him why it's coming to him in particular: because you are my devotee and my friend, and this is a deep secret. Arjuna, being Arjuna, hears a problem. Your birth was recent, he says. The sun's was long ago. How could you have taught him? Krishna's answer is the turn of the chapter. Many births have passed, he says, for me and for you. I know them all. You don't. Then he describes his own coming. Though unborn, and the Lord of all beings, he says he comes into being through his own power, his own maya. And he says when: whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet. Here's the link to our word. In the next verse, Krishna speaks of his birth and his action, his karma, as divine. Whoever truly knows them, he says, isn't born again when they leave the body, but comes to him. So the one teaching the yoga of action is also acting, taking birth, entering the world, doing the work. The commentators read his coming differently. Shankara speaks of the Lord appearing to take a body by his own maya, his power, while remaining unborn. Ramanuja insists the Lord's births are real, taken freely by his own will and not forced on him by karma, as ours are. Both are reading the same verse. And the shape of the chapter holds either way: the teaching of action comes down a chain of people, and it's renewed by one who acts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma handed down: the sun, Manu, Ikshvaku, a teaching lost and told again by one whose birth and action are divine. What did you pass on? Day nine hundred sixty-six, the end of a week.

Before the first bite, in some Hindu homes, someone says a line in Sanskrit over the plate. Brahmarpanam brahma havir. It comes from chapter four of the Gita, and it's an odd thing to say before dinner, because it's a verse about a fire sacrifice. The offering is Brahman. The thing offered is Brahman. It's poured into the fire, which is Brahman, by the one offering, who is Brahman. A meal, a fire, a giver, all one. Today, the middle of chapter four, and how a single act can be seen all the way through.
screen: `A LINE SAID OVER THE PLATE.` → `THE OFFERING IS BRAHMAN.` → `ONE ACT, SEEN ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: A few verses before the meal verse, Krishna sets a puzzle. What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise, he says, are confused about this. Then the answer: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people, and does all their work in yoga. Shankara reads this as seeing that the Self never acts, even while the body is busy. Ramanuja reads it as seeing knowledge of the self alive inside work done without attachment. Then Krishna describes such a person. Their acts have been burned in the fire of knowledge. They've let go of clinging to the fruit, they're always content, depending on nothing, and though they keep acting, they do nothing at all. And then the meal verse. Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in the act goes to Brahman. Here's what's happened to our word since chapter three began. In chapter three, karma was action you can't avoid, done as offering, turning the wheel. Then action done for the world, the way Janaka did it. Then action handed down through a chain of teachers, and taken up by God. And now, action seen so clearly that the doer, the deed and the fire turn out to be one thing. Later in the chapter Krishna says it plainly: as a kindled fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash. Look back over the week. Tagore's flute, emptied and filled. God in the dust with the pathmaker. A mind waking into thought and action. And the Gita's long answer to Arjuna's complaint: you can't stop acting, so learn to see what acting is.

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind the last thing you ate, or the next thing you will. Go through it the way the verse does. The food. The hands that will lift it. The hunger it goes into. The one who's eating. Don't try to believe anything about it. Just look at each part, slowly, and then at all of them together as one act. If you pray, you can say the verse's opening words, brahmarpanam brahma havir, or a grace from your own tradition. If not, simply rest in the whole act at once. The bell holds the time.
Karma. In chapter four, action seen so clearly that the offering, the fire and the one who offers are one, and the act itself turns to ash in the fire of knowledge.
Your line: the offering, the fire and the one who offers. Today, before one meal, pause long enough to see the food, the hands and the hunger as a single act. Day nine hundred sixty-six.
